analysis.one_liner: Cuts the corporate tax rate permanently while most individual tax cuts expire after a few years.
analysis.headline: The Senate's version of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act was reported to the Senate floor on November 28, 2017, and its substance was enacted that December through the parallel bill H.R. 1 on party-line votes, becoming law over every Democrat's objection.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill rewrites the federal tax code. It permanently cuts the corporate tax rate from 35% to 20%, permanently repeals the corporate minimum tax, and creates a large new deduction for owners of partnerships, LLCs, and other pass-through businesses. For individuals, it lowers rates and raises the standard deduction and child tax credit, but those provisions mostly expire after 2025, and it also repeals the penalty for going without health insurance, ends deductions for state and local taxes and personal exemptions, and opens part of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge to oil and gas drilling.
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations and their shareholders get the permanent tax cut. Owners of pass-through businesses — law firms, real-estate partnerships, medical practices, closely held companies — get a new deduction worth up to 20% of their business income through 2025. High earners benefit from a lower top rate, suspension of the individual minimum tax, and a doubled estate tax exemption. Ordinary working families get lower rates, a bigger standard deduction, and a larger child credit, but those changes are temporary and are offset for many by the loss of personal exemptions and, in high-tax states, the state and local tax deduction.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Corporations, business owners, and high earners

how_it_helps.text: Permanently cuts the top corporate tax rate from 35% to a flat 20% and permanently repeals the corporate alternative minimum tax.

Creates a new deduction for business income of pass-through entities (partnerships, S corporations, LLCs, sole proprietorships), limited largely to owners above roughly $250,000 in taxable income and phased out for high-income service businesses.

Lowers individual tax rates (top rate falls from 39.6% to 38.5% in this version), roughly doubles the standard deduction to $12,000 single / $18,000 married, and raises the child tax credit to $2,000 with a new $500 credit for other dependents.
Suspends the individual alternative minimum tax, doubles the estate tax exemption, and lifts the overall limit on itemized deductions.

Provides targeted relief provisions: disaster-tax relief for 2016 Louisiana flood victims, tax-free treatment of student loans discharged for death or disability, a doubled teacher classroom-expense deduction, and expanded ABLE savings accounts for people with disabilities.

analysis.who_pays: The bill is not fully paid for; its cost is added to the federal debt, which future taxpayers bear. Families in high-tax states lose the deduction for state and local taxes, larger families lose the personal exemption, homeowners lose the deduction for home-equity loan interest, and movers lose the moving-expense deduction. People who buy their own health insurance face a destabilized market after the individual mandate penalty is repealed. The slowest-growing inflation measure (chained CPI) is applied to tax brackets, so tax thresholds rise more slowly over time, quietly raising taxes in real terms. The bill also mandates an oil and gas leasing program in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's Coastal Plain and sales from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve.
analysis.who_pays_short: Future taxpayers, high-tax-state families, insurance buyers

drawbacks.text: Most provisions affecting individuals — the rate cuts, bigger standard deduction, and child tax credit — expire after 2025, while the corporate rate cut is permanent, so average family taxes are scheduled to rise in later years even as business taxes stay low.
It repeals the Affordable Care Act's individual mandate penalty, which removes relatively healthy customers from insurance markets and puts upward pressure on premiums for the people who remain.

It eliminates the personal exemption (worth about $4,150 per family member) and the deduction for state and local taxes, so many families — especially larger families and residents of high-tax states — see smaller cuts or tax increases, while the child credit increase ($1,000) does not fully make up the difference.
It switches tax-code inflation adjustments to the slower-growing chained CPI, so tax brackets, deductions, and credits shrink relative to prices over time.

It directs the Interior Department to open the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's Coastal Plain to oil and gas leasing and the Energy Department to sell oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, with environmental costs that the bill's supporters weighed against revenue.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Most working families did get a near-term tax cut from the lower rates, bigger standard deduction, and larger child credit, and that was real money in the near years. The honest trade-off is that those family provisions are temporary while the deepest cuts — the corporate rate, the corporate minimum tax repeal, and the pass-through deduction — go to businesses and owners, some permanently. The bill is financed by borrowing, the mandate repeal raises premiums for people buying their own coverage, and the changes that fall on individuals in later years (chained CPI, expiring credits, lost exemptions) work in the opposite direction. On the design alone, the benefits are weighted toward concentrated interests with family relief as the temporary front end.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate never voted on S. 1 itself; leadership instead used its text as the Senate version of the parallel bill H.R. 1, which the Senate passed 51-49 on December 2, 2017, the House passed on party-line votes on December 19-20, 2017, and President Trump signed into law on December 22, 2017.

narrative.text: The Senate Budget Committee reported this original reconciliation measure on November 28, 2017, and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders the same day.

As a reconciliation bill under the fiscal 2018 budget resolution, it needed only a simple majority in the Senate rather than the usual 60-vote threshold, which is why it could pass without any Democratic votes.
The bill cuts the corporate tax rate to 20% permanently, while most individual provisions expire after 2025.
The bill repeals the individual health insurance mandate penalty and directs oil and gas leasing in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge.
No Senate Democrats supported the measure in either chamber's votes, and it passed the Senate 51-49 with a single Republican defection and the House 224-201 on final passage in December 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporations, owners of pass-through businesses, and high-income households are better off because of what actually happened: they received the largest and most permanent tax cuts, while the version that passed left the individual provisions temporary and added roughly $1.5 trillion to projected deficits that all taxpayers inherit.

for.name: Sen. Mike Enzi
for.role: Chair, Senate Budget Committee (introduced and reported the original reconciliation bill)
for.what_they_did: Introduced S. 1 on November 28, 2017 and reported it from the Budget Committee to the Senate calendar as the majority's tax reconciliation vehicle.

for.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
for.what_they_did: Brought the tax reconciliation bill to the Senate floor and managed its passage through the chamber in December 2017, bypassing S. 1's own calendar placement by attaching the text to H.R. 1.

for.name: President Donald Trump
for.what_they_did: Pressed Congress to pass the tax bill and signed the final law on December 22, 2017.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Led unanimous Democratic opposition to the tax bill in the Senate, opposing the corporate cuts and the individual mandate repeal.

against.name: Sen. Bob Corker
against.role: Senator from Tennessee (the lone Republican 'no' vote in the Senate)
against.what_they_did: Voted against the Senate tax bill on the floor, citing its projected addition to the federal deficit.

against.name: House and Senate Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted as a bloc against the tax bill in both the Senate (December 2017) and the House (December 2017), offering no votes on the version that became law.

sides.party_line_note: The vote was almost purely by party: the Senate passed the bill 51-49 with every Democrat and independent opposed and one Republican defecting, and final House passage was 224-201 with 12 Republicans joining all opposing Democrats.

industries.note: The bill permanently cuts the corporate rate from 35% to 20% and repeals the corporate minimum tax — the largest and longest-lasting provisions in the law. The cost arrives as added federal debt and, over time, as expiring family tax breaks.

industries.industry: Owners of pass-through businesses (partnerships, LLCs, S corporations, sole proprietors)
industries.note: Owners get a new deduction worth up to 20% of qualified business income, with rules that phase out the benefit for high-income service professionals above about $250,000 in taxable income. This is one of the most-used provisions by wealthy business owners.
The top rate drops, the individual minimum tax is suspended, the estate tax exemption doubles, and limits on itemized deductions are lifted — all favoring households with large incomes and estates.

The bill directs the Interior Department to run an oil and gas leasing program in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's Coastal Plain and the Energy Department to sell oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, opening a protected area to drilling for revenue.

Repealing the individual mandate penalty removes healthier, subsidized-market customers, shrinking insurers' risk pools; many insurers respond with higher premiums, which fall mainly on people who buy their own coverage.

industries.industry: State and local governments in high-tax states
industries.note: Suspending the federal deduction for state and local taxes makes residents' state and local taxes more expensive after-tax, adding pressure on governments in high-tax states that had relied on the deduction.
